results.name: round_target_bonus_no_round_examples
results.description: Among sets containing no multiple of 10, yes rate for targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes rate for other targets; observed above null means people say yes to round numbers more than the model predicts when nothing in the examples supports them (a round-number salience), below null means less.
results.code:
# name: round_target_bonus_no_round_examples
# description: Among sets containing no multiple of 10, yes rate for targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes rate for other targets; observed above null means people say yes to round numbers more than the model predicts when nothing in the examples supports them (a round-number salience), below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parts = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    has_round = np.nansum((np.mod(parts, 10) == 0).astype(float), axis=1) > 0
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    keep = ~has_round
    rt = keep & (t % 10 == 0)
    ot = keep & (t % 10 != 0)
    if rt.sum() == 0 or ot.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[rt].mean() - r[ot].mean())

results.name: above_vs_below_range_asymmetry
results.description: Among sets with 2+ examples, yes rate for targets above the largest example minus yes rate for targets below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward more than downward relative to the model's symmetric ranges and rules, below null means more downward.
results.code:
# name: above_vs_below_range_asymmetry
# description: Among sets with 2+ examples, yes rate for targets above the largest example minus yes rate for targets below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward more than downward relative to the model's symmetric ranges and rules, below null means more downward.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parts = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    mx = parts.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    mn = parts.min(axis=1).to_numpy()
    multi = (s.str.count(",") >= 1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    up = multi & (t > mx)
    dn = multi & (t < mn)
    if up.sum() == 0 or dn.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[up].mean() - r[dn].mean())

results.name: within_set_target_magnitude_slope
results.description: Least-squares slope of the set-demeaned yes response on set-demeaned target/100 (pooled over all trials); observed below null means people favour small targets within a set more than the model predicts (a magnitude/small-number bias), above null means they favour large targets more.
results.code:
# name: within_set_target_magnitude_slope
# description: Least-squares slope of the set-demeaned yes response on set-demeaned target/100 (pooled over all trials); observed below null means people favour small targets within a set more than the model predicts (a magnitude/small-number bias), above null means they favour large targets more.
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(float) / 100.0
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    key = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    tc = t - t.groupby(key).transform("mean")
    rc = r - r.groupby(key).transform("mean")
    den = float((tc * tc).sum())
    if den <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((tc * rc).sum() / den)

results.name: leading_digit_match_gap
results.description: Among sets with 2+ examples, for two-digit targets whose final digit matches no example, yes rate when the target's tens digit equals some example's tens digit minus yes rate when it equals none; observed above null means people generalise along shared leading digits (same decade) more than the model's ranges and contains-digit rules predict, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: leading_digit_match_gap
# description: Among sets with 2+ examples, for two-digit targets whose final digit matches no example, yes rate when the target's tens digit equals some example's tens digit minus yes rate when it equals none; observed above null means people generalise along shared leading digits (same decade) more than the model's ranges and contains-digit rules predict, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parts = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(parts)
    ex_tens = np.where(valid & (parts >= 10) & (parts < 100), np.floor(parts / 10), -1)
    ex_ones = np.where(valid, np.mod(parts, 10), -1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    tt = (t // 10).astype(float)
    to = (t % 10).astype(float)
    tens_match = (ex_tens == tt[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    ones_match = (ex_ones == to[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    member = (parts == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    multi = (s.str.count(",") >= 1).to_numpy()
    base = multi & (t >= 10) & (t < 100) & ~ones_match & ~member
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = base & tens_match
    b = base & ~tens_match
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: singleton_multiple_of_example_gap
results.description: Among single-example sets with example 2-50, yes rate for targets that are other multiples of the example minus yes rate for non-multiples; observed above null means after one example people already generalise to its times table more than the model predicts (model's weak single-example commitment is too weak), below null means less.
results.code:
# name: singleton_multiple_of_example_gap
# description: Among single-example sets with example 2-50, yes rate for targets that are other multiples of the example minus yes rate for non-multiples; observed above null means after one example people already generalise to its times table more than the model predicts (model's weak single-example commitment is too weak), below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = (~s.str.contains(",")).to_numpy()
    x = pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce").fillna(0).to_numpy().astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ok = single & (x >= 2) & (x <= 50) & (t != x)
    xs = np.where(x > 0, x, 1)
    mult = (t % xs == 0)
    a = ok & mult
    b = ok & ~mult
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: set_size_three_vs_four_yes_gap
results.description: Overall yes rate on 3-example sets minus yes rate on 4-example sets; observed above null means people generalise more after three examples (and tighten more at four) than the model's set-size evidence weighting predicts, below null means the model overstates the 3-vs-4 difference.

results.name: multi_set_nearest_example_gradient
results.description: Among sets with 2+ examples and targets not in the set, yes rate for targets 1-3 away from the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 4-15 away; observed above null means people show a sharper local similarity gradient around individual examples than the model's ranges and rules produce, below null means a flatter one.
results.code:
# name: multi_set_nearest_example_gradient
# description: Among sets with 2+ examples and targets not in the set, yes rate for targets 1-3 away from the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 4-15 away; observed above null means people show a sharper local similarity gradient around individual examples than the model's ranges and rules produce, below null means a flatter one.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parts = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.abs(parts - t[:, None])
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), np.inf, d)
    dmin = d.min(axis=1)
    multi = (s.str.count(",") >= 1).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    near = multi & (dmin >= 1) & (dmin <= 3)
    mid = multi & (dmin >= 4) & (dmin <= 15)
    if near.sum() == 0 or mid.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[mid].mean())

results.name: between_set_yes_rate_variance
results.description: Variance across sets (sets with at least 10 trials) of each set's overall yes rate; observed above null means sets differ more in how broadly people generalise (some sets near all-yes, others near all-no) than the model predicts, below null means the model exaggerates set-to-set differences in breadth.
